## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (FRDD) in age-in-days.

Rationale  
•  Medicare eligibility (the “treatment”) jumps sharply at the first day of the month a person turns 65.  
•  The running variable (exact age) is continuous and observed to the day, so we can compare patients who are only a few days younger than 65 with those a few days older.  
•  Because not every 65-year-old is on Medicare and a few <65s have Medicare (e.g., the disabled), the design is fuzzy, i.e., the cutoff produces a large discontinuity in the probability of insurance rather than deterministic treatment.  
•  For acutely ill ER patients, self-selection around the cutoff is impossible; underlying health trends are smooth in age at the daily or weekly horizon.  
Hence an FRDD isolates the causal effect of gaining near-universal, fee-for-service coverage on treatment intensity and mortality.

## 2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
Treated = having Medicare primary coverage (binary).  
We will also estimate the intent-to-treat (ITT) effect of “age ≥ 65.”

Control group  
Patients whose age-in-days is just below 65 (e.g., 64.75–64.999 years) serve as the counterfactual.

Running variable and cutoff  
Running variable: age_in_days = discharge_date – date_of_birth (in days).  
Cutoff: c = 65 × 365.25 = 23,741.25 days.  
Because Medicare starts on the 1st of the month one turns 65, we will define a precise cutoff at the first day of the 65th birth-month and adjust exposure on the left side symmetrically (±30, ±60, ±90 days, etc.).

Treatment timing / event date  
Treatment starts the day the patient becomes eligible for Medicare. Our analysis window is symmetric around that day; e.g., a ±180-day bandwidth for the main specification.

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Continuity of potential outcomes.  
Absent Medicare eligibility, the conditional expectation of treatment intensity and mortality evolves smoothly in age at the cutoff.  
• Plausible: no physiological or medical-practice break exactly at 65.

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable.  
Patients cannot time heart attacks or strokes to the exact day relative to their 65th birthday.  
• Plausible for non-deferrable ER admissions; we will confirm with a McCrary density test.

A3. Monotonic first stage (eligibility → coverage).  
Crossing the cutoff weakly increases the chance of Medicare coverage for everyone.  
• Plausible: virtually nobody loses coverage at 65.

A4. Stable composition within bandwidth.  
The mix of diagnoses, hospital types, and patient demographics changes smoothly in age.  
• Plausible; to be checked by covariate balance tests.

## 4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  

1. Concurrent retirement/social-security changes at 65  
   • Threat: Retirement could alter post-hospital care or mortality.  
   • Mitigation:  
     – Focus on non-deferrable emergency diagnoses that occur independently of labor-supply decisions.  
     – Control for employment-linked diagnosis mix; run placebo RD among patients with employer insurance to show flat outcomes.  
     – Narrow bandwidth (±60 days) where retirement behavior is unlikely to change abruptly.

2. Measurement error in age or eligibility month  
   • Threat: Blurs the cutoff, attenuating estimates.  
   • Mitigation:  
     – Use age in days from DOB and discharge date (both recorded).  
     – Drop observations with imputed or suspect DOBs.  
     – Use “month of 65th birthday” rule to define eligibility precisely.

3. Differential sample selection by insurance pre-admission  
   • Threat: Privately insured <65s might seek care at different hospitals than Medicare ≥65s.  
   • Mitigation:  
     – Limit to ER admissions (entrance through emergency department) to hold constant the access point.  
     – Show hospital fixed-effects–based RD (running variable within hospital) yields similar results.  
     – Check balance in hospital share at the cutoff.

## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
############################################################
# 0. Packages
############################################################
library(data.table)   # fast I/O
library(lubridate)    # date handling
library(fixest)       # fast OLS/IV
library(rdrobust)     # RD estimators
library(ggplot2)

############################################################
# 1. Load discharge data (CSV assumed)
############################################################
d <- fread("california_discharge_1992_2002.csv")

############################################################
# 2. Basic variable construction
############################################################
# Dates
d[, dob        := ymd(date_of_birth)]
d[, dis_date   := ymd(discharge_date)]

# Age in days at discharge
d[, age_days   := as.numeric(dis_date - dob)]

# Medicare eligibility start: first day of birth month when turning 65
d[, elig_date  := floor_date(dob + years(65), "month")]
# Running variable: days from cutoff (negative = pre-65)
d[, runvar     := as.numeric(dis_date - elig_date)]

# Treatment variables
d[, medicare   := (primary_insurance == "Medicare")]
d[, post65     := (runvar >= 0)]               # ITT indicator

# Sample restriction: non-deferrable ER admits, age 60–70
nondeferrable_codes <- fread("nondeferrable_dx.csv")$icd9
d <- d[route_of_admission == "ER" &
       primary_icd9 %in% nondeferrable_codes &
       age_days/365.25 >= 60 & age_days/365.25 <= 70]

############################################################
# 3. Main FRDD specification (±180-day bandwidth)
############################################################
bw <- 180           # bandwidth in days
sample <- d[abs(runvar) <= bw]

# First stage: effect on Medicare coverage
fs <- feols(medicare ~ post65 + poly(runvar, 1) | 0, data = sample)
summary(fs)

# Second stage / 2SLS for treatment intensity (log charges)
yvar <- "log(list_charges)"
iv_main <- feols(as.formula(paste(yvar, "~ 1 | 0 | post65 ~ medicare + poly(runvar,1)")),
                 data = sample)
summary(iv_main)

# Reduced form for 30-day mortality
d[, death30 := (death_date <= dis_date + days(30))]
rf <- feols(death30 ~ post65 + poly(runvar,1), data = sample)
summary(rf)

############################################################
# 4. rdrobust as robustness (local linear, triangular, fuzzy)
############################################################
rd_out <- rdrobust(y = sample[[yvar]], x = sample$runvar,
                   c = 0, fuzzy = sample$medicare)
summary(rd_out)

############################################################
# 5. Placebo cutoff robustness at age 64
############################################################
# Shift running variable by -365 days (placebo cutoff one year earlier)
d[, runvar_placebo := runvar + 365]
placebo <- d[abs(runvar_placebo) <= bw]
placebo_est <- feols(death30 ~ I(runvar_placebo>=0) + poly(runvar_placebo,1),
                     data = placebo)
summary(placebo_est)
```

Notes  
• `poly(runvar,1)` gives a linear control. Replace by higher-order polynomials or local linear kernels as robustness.  
• For the IV in `fixest`, the syntax is `y ~ controls | fixed.effects | endog ~ instr`.

## 6. Expected Results  
Economic intuition suggests that fee-for-service Medicare reduces financial barriers and utilization controls, leading hospitals to provide slightly more intensive care (longer stays, more procedures) to marginal ≥65 ER patients. Enhanced treatment should translate into lower mortality provided additional care is effective.

Prior on magnitude  
• 30-day mortality baseline for severe ER cases ≈ 6 %.  
• A 60 p.p. increase in generous coverage might lower mortality by ~1 p.p. (≈ 15 % relative decline).  
• Treatment intensity (log list-charges) is expected to rise by ~5–10 %.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (FRDD)  
C1: Visible first-stage discontinuity in treatment (Medicare coverage)  … 1  
C2: Continuity of predetermined covariates at cutoff                   … 0.8  
C3: No manipulation of running variable (McCrary test)                 … 1  
C4: Robust to bandwidths & polynomial order                            … 0.8  
C5: Placebo cutoffs show null effects                                  … 1  

Average score ≈ 0.92 → high internal validity, pending empirical tests.
